```{r setup}
library(dplyr)
library(gt)

period_results <- readRDS("../data-raw/validation_period_results.rds")
row_results <- readRDS("../data-raw/validation_row_results.rds")
process_log <- readr::read_csv("../data-raw/process_log.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

n_tables <- process_log |> filter(status == "ok") |> nrow()

all_results <- bind_rows(
  period_results |> mutate(family = "Period (column-wise)"),
  row_results |> mutate(family = "Row (row-wise)")
)

fmt_num <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)

# table_id is "<dataset>/<8-char-hash>__<slug>" - strip the hash and
# truncate for display so wide gt tables don't overflow the PDF page width
# (quarto/LaTeX silently clips columns that don't fit rather than wrapping)
short_slug <- function(table_id, max_chars = 38) {
  slug <- sub("^[^/]+/[a-z0-9]{8}__", "", table_id)
  slug <- gsub("_", " ", slug)
  ifelse(nchar(slug) > max_chars, paste0(substr(slug, 1, max_chars - 1), "…"), slug)
}
```

## Purpose and methodology

This report checks the internal arithmetic consistency of the `r n_tables`
tidy tables produced by this project's ingest pipeline from IRCC's and
IRB's open data. Two independent families of checks are run on every
processed table:

**Column-wise, within a row** — for a single row category (e.g. Ontario,
Female), do its own figures add up across time?

- Do a quarter's three monthly values sum to its published quarter total?
- Do a year's monthly values sum to its published annual total (where a
  table publishes both)?
- Do a year's quarterly totals sum to its published annual total (where a
  table publishes both)?

**Row-wise, within a period column** — for a single point in time (e.g.
January 2015), do a table's nested row categories add up correctly?

- Do a group's detail rows (e.g. the provinces within a group) sum to the
  group's published subtotal row?
- Do a table's top-level subtotal rows sum to its published grand total?

Row-wise checks only apply to tables with a nested row hierarchy (IRCC's
"pivot" Excel tables); flat, already-tidy tables have nothing to check
here since they have no subtotal rows.

### Why exact equality isn't the bar

IRCC and IRB round every published figure to the nearest multiple of 5,
independently at every level of a table, and suppress ("`--`") any value
between 0 and 5 to protect privacy. That means even a perfectly correct
table's components essentially never sum to *exactly* their published
total — only to within rounding and suppression noise. A check that
required exact equality would flag nearly everything, which would be
useless.

Instead, each comparison is scored against a conservative tolerance band:

$$
\text{tolerance} = 2.5 \times (n_{\text{terms}} + 1) + 5 \times n_{\text{suppressed}}
$$

- $2.5 \times (n_{\text{terms}} + 1)$ allows for each summed component's own
  rounding error (up to $\pm 2.5$) plus the total/subtotal cell's own
  rounding error.
- $5 \times n_{\text{suppressed}}$ allows for each suppressed ("`--`")
  component, which could be as large as 5 but is treated as 0 in the
  observed sum.

A comparison is marked:

- **pass** — the difference between the published total and the sum of its
  parts is within tolerance.
- **anomaly** — the difference exceeds tolerance, flagged for review.
- **not checkable** — the total/subtotal cell itself is suppressed, so
  there is nothing to compare against.
- **not applicable** — the check doesn't apply to this table (see
  "stock" tables below).

## Overall results

```{r overall-summary}
all_results |>
  count(family, status) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = status, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Checks by family and outcome") |>
  fmt_number(columns = where(is.numeric), decimals = 0, sep_mark = ",")
```

```{r check-type-summary}
all_results |>
  count(check_type, status) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = status, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Checks by type and outcome")
```

```{r anomaly-rate}
n_anomaly <- sum(all_results$status == "anomaly")
n_checked <- sum(all_results$status %in% c("pass", "anomaly"))
anomaly_rate <- if (n_checked > 0) round(100 * n_anomaly / n_checked, 3) else 0
```

Of `r format(n_checked, big.mark = ",")` checks where the published total
was not itself suppressed, `r format(n_anomaly, big.mark = ",")`
(`r anomaly_rate`%) fell outside the rounding/suppression tolerance and are
flagged as anomalies below.

## Anomalies by table

```{r anomalies-by-table}
anomaly_by_table <- all_results |>
  filter(status == "anomaly") |>
  mutate(dataset = sub("/.*$", "", table_id), table = short_slug(table_id)) |>
  count(dataset, table, family, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 25)

if (nrow(anomaly_by_table) == 0) {
  cat("No anomalies were flagged in any table.")
} else {
  anomaly_by_table |>
    gt() |>
    tab_header(title = "Tables with the most flagged anomalies (top 25)") |>
    cols_label(n = "Anomalies") |>
    cols_width(dataset ~ px(140), table ~ px(230), family ~ px(110), n ~ px(70)) |>
    tab_options(table.font.size = 9)
}
```

## Anomaly detail

Several source tables cover the same underlying data under different
resource names (a known gap in the manifest dedup - see the project
README), so the same anomaly often appears identically in more than one
processed table. The list below is deduplicated by its numeric signature
(check type, period, published total, sum of parts) so each *distinct*
anomaly is shown once, with a count of how many tables exhibit it and one
example table:

```{r anomaly-detail}
detail <- all_results |>
  filter(status == "anomaly") |>
  mutate(excess = abs(diff) - tolerance) |>
  group_by(check_type, period_label, total_value, sum_of_parts, diff, tolerance, excess) |>
  summarise(n_tables = dplyr::n_distinct(table_id),
            example_table = dplyr::first(short_slug(table_id)), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(excess)) |>
  slice_head(n = 25) |>
  transmute(
    check_type, period_label,
    total = fmt_num(total_value), sum_of_parts = fmt_num(sum_of_parts),
    diff = fmt_num(diff), n_tables, example_table
  )

if (nrow(detail) == 0) {
  cat("No anomalies to show.")
} else {
  detail |>
    gt() |>
    tab_header(title = "Largest distinct anomalies (top 25 by signature)") |>
    cols_label(
      check_type = "Check", period_label = "Period",
      total = "Published total", sum_of_parts = "Sum of parts", diff = "Difference",
      n_tables = "# tables", example_table = "Example table"
    ) |>
    cols_width(check_type ~ px(90), period_label ~ px(75), total ~ px(65),
               sum_of_parts ~ px(65), diff ~ px(65), n_tables ~ px(50),
               example_table ~ px(150)) |>
    tab_options(table.font.size = 8)
}
```

## Two investigated sources of anomalies

Both patterns below were found by tracing the largest flagged anomalies
back to their source spreadsheets. Both are validator-methodology
mismatches rather than errors in IRCC's or IRB's published figures.

### 1. "Valid permit" (stock) tables aren't additive across months - fixed, not just flagged

```{r stock-tables}
stock_checks <- period_results |> filter(status == "not_applicable")
n_stock_checks <- nrow(stock_checks)
n_stock_tables <- n_distinct(stock_checks$table_id)
pct_of_original <- round(100 * n_stock_checks / (n_stock_checks + sum(all_results$status == "anomaly")), 1)
```

Most IRCC tables measure a *flow*: permits that became effective in a
given month, which are naturally additive (Jan + Feb + Mar = Q1). But
`r n_stock_tables` tables - "Study permit holders **with a valid
permit** by province/territory..." and its siblings - measure a *stock*:
how many permit holders had a currently-valid permit as of that month.
Stock counts are not additive across time (the same person holding a
valid permit in January, February, and March would be triple-counted),
so the "Q# Total" column in these tables is not a sum of its three
months - checking one against the other in the same way naturally
produces a large, consistent mismatch. Spot-checking a specific
row (Alberta / Albania, 2018 Q2) shows the mechanism directly: Apr = 15,
May = 15, Jun = 15, **Q2 Total = 15** - the quarter figure equals each
individual month, not their sum.

This is not a data quality problem - it means the `month_to_quarter` /
`quarter_to_year` checks simply don't apply to stock-type tables.
Rather than guess from table titles (not every stock table's name says
"valid permit" - two of the five affected here are older legacy exports
that don't), `R/validate_utils.R::reclassify_stock_tables()` detects the
pattern directly from the numbers: any table whose `month_to_quarter`
sum-of-parts runs consistently ~3x its published total gets those checks
relabelled **not applicable** rather than left as false-positive
anomalies. `r format(n_stock_checks, big.mark = ",")` checks across
`r n_stock_tables` tables were reclassified this way - without this
fix, they would have made up `r pct_of_original`% of everything flagged
in this report.

### 2. Appended second breakdowns (row-wise)

```{r doubled-grand-totals}
gt_checks <- row_results |> filter(check_type == "grand_total")
gt_checks <- gt_checks |> mutate(ratio = sum_of_parts / total_value)
doubled <- gt_checks |> filter(!is.na(ratio), ratio > 1.5, ratio < 2.5)
n_doubled_tables <- length(unique(doubled$table_id))
```

Separately, some IRCC Excel sheets append a **second, independently-grouped
breakdown** below the main table - sharing the same grand total - rather
than publishing it as a separate table. For example, "Work permit holders
for Humanitarian and Compassionate purposes by gender, age..." lists a
full gender → age breakdown first, then appends a second, flat age-only
breakdown underneath, both summing to the same overall total. The current
parser does not detect this second-table boundary, so it treats the
appended rows as more members of the same row hierarchy - which
mechanically causes a subtotal/grand-total check to see roughly double
the true count.

`r nrow(doubled)` of the `r nrow(gt_checks)` grand-total checks
(across `r n_doubled_tables` table(s)) show almost exactly a 2x
sum-to-total ratio, the signature of this pattern. The remaining flagged
row-wise anomalies - particularly the elevated rate at `row_subtotal_level_1`
and `row_subtotal_level_3` shown above - warrant a manual look against
their source spreadsheets; some may be further instances of this same
appended-table pattern (in tables with deeper nesting, an appended second
breakdown surfaces at whichever row level it was inserted at, not
necessarily level 1), and some may be genuine artifacts worth tracing
further. This report flags them; it does not attempt to auto-correct them.

## Coverage notes

- `not_checkable` results (total/subtotal itself suppressed) and
  `not_applicable` results (stock-type tables, see above) are both
  excluded from the anomaly rate above since there is nothing to verify
  in either case - neither is evidence of a problem.
- Row-wise checks only run against tables with a nested row hierarchy
  (IRCC's pivot-format Excel tables). Flat/already-tidy tables (most CSVs,
  and both IRB tables) have no subtotal rows to check and so contribute
  no row-wise results.
- Column-wise year-level checks (`month_to_year`, `quarter_to_year`) only
  run where a table actually publishes an annual total alongside its
  monthly/quarterly breakdown, which most IRCC tables don't (the current,
  still-in-progress year is the main exception).
- Row-wise anomaly rates vary noticeably by nesting level (see the
  check-type table above) - levels 2 and 4 are consistently clean while
  levels 1 and 3 run higher, concentrated in a handful of tables rather
  than spread evenly. That unevenness is itself a useful signal for where
  to look first.
